6	## The document viewer — `internal/viewer` + `internal/ui/viewer`
7	
8	One document, read-only. A **destination with three producers**, the shape the
9	security view already has:
10	
11	| Producer | Key | Source | Document |
12	|---|---|---|---|
13	| `workspaces` | `enter` on a file | `viewer.FileSource` | detected |
14	| `containers` | `enter` | `inspectSource` | JSON |
15	| `containers` | `L` | `logsSource` | log |
16	
17	Two axes, and they are the whole interface: **display** (`f`) and **highlight**
18	(`c`). "Plain text" is text with the colour off; a display of its own for it
19	would be one screen reachable two ways — what §3.9 removed from the secret
20	backend and what took the `:theme` command with it.
21	
22	**`f` is one axis with one meaning: the document as it is, against the one view
23	its kind derives from it.** A kind derives at most one — a tree when
24	`Kind.Structured()`, a rendered form when `Kind.Renderable()`, never both, and
25	`TestNoKindHasTwoDerivedDisplays` says so. That is what keeps the toggle binary
26	at every moment even though `display` has three values, and why `Model.derived()`
27	is one function rather than a switch at each of the three call sites that need
28	it: `f`, the opening display and `GetShortcuts` have to give the same answer or
29	the view offers a display it will then refuse to show (Rule 130).
30	
31	| Kind | `f` switches between | Derived by |
32	|---|---|---|
33	| JSON, XML | the tree and the text | `parseJSON` / `parseXML` |
34	| Markdown | the rendered form and the raw source | `RenderMarkdown` |
35	| everything else | nothing — `f` is hidden (Rule 130) | — |
36

38	nothing more. Every marker `RenderMarkdown` takes off is one chroma *already
39	identified* — a heading, a strong, an emphasis, a strikethrough, a bullet, a
40	quote prefix, a fence. Nothing there parses, and nothing decides from what a
41	character looks like: that is why **links, tables and thematic breaks survive
42	untouched**. A link's `[` and `]` arrive as bare `Text`, indistinguishable from a
43	bracket in prose, so rebuilding one would be exactly the guesswork this package
44	refuses everywhere else — the link text and its URL are coloured apart instead,
45	which is most of what rendering it would have bought.
46	
47	The one invariant it breaks is Tokenize's: **the concatenation no longer
48	reproduces the input**. It is the point. Everything downstream copes because it
49	reads the tokens rather than the document — `splitTokenLines` rebuilds each
50	line's plain text from them, so the search filters and highlights what is
51	actually on screen. The raw display is still the source to the character, which
52	is what makes the omissions above limits rather than losses.
53	
54	`c` stays orthogonal to all of it: turning the colour off in a rendered document
55	does **not** put the asterisks back. The rendering is a display, the colouring is
56	a colouring, and a `c` that revealed markers would be the second way to reach one
57	screen that the paragraph above rules out.
58	
59	**A document carries its `Source`, not its bytes.** Reload, follow and the
60	timestamps toggle are questions for the origin. Three **single-method** optional
61	interfaces, probed by type assertion like `FooterView`:
62	
63	| Interface | Unlocks | Implemented by |
64	|---|---|---|
65	| `Timestamped` | `t` | `logsSource` |
66	| `Followable` | `F` | `logsSource` |
67	| `Pageable` | `V` | `logsSource` |

71	half-satisfied state. `WithTimestamps` returns a *new* source rather than
72	mutating one, so nothing is shared with a command in flight (Rule 110).

75	command.** It used to return an `*exec.Cmd` run through `tea.ExecProcess`, on
76	the argument that `docker logs -f` already does this and re-implementing it

84	Following is therefore `ctrl+r` on a timer: the same `loadCmd`, the same

87	
88	- **The generation ends a loop, not the flag.** `tea.Tick` blocks its whole
89	  interval, so a tick scheduled before `F` stopped still arrives; restarting
90	  before it lands would leave two loops reading for the life of the view.
91	  `stopFollowing` bumps `followGen` and is the one place following is turned
92	  off — `esc` included, since the router keeps this view and a loop left behind

94	- **A followed document lands at the bottom**, where the new lines are. Every

108	destroys exactly what the log was opened for. The chain breaks on a blank line —
109	otherwise one ERROR colours half the file. A line before any level is

111	discovered: a genuinely unrelated unlevelled line after an INFO goes with it.
112	
113	`v` cycles a **minimum** (`all → trace → debug → info → warn → error`), not four
114	toggles: that is what "verbosity" means and log levels are monotone. One
115	`FilterBar` token (Rule 136), gone at `all`.

117	**Six kinds are declared, never sniffed**: `KindLog`, `KindYAML`, `KindTOML`,
118	`KindMarkdown`, `KindDockerfile` and `KindShell`. "This looks like a log" is not
119	decidable, and neither is "this looks like YAML" — a file opening with `---` is
120	Markdown front matter as often as a YAML stream, and a `[section]` line is prose
121	in half the files that hold one. The registry `provider` field is the precedent.
122	JSON and XML keep a content sniff, but only for a file with **no extension**: a
123	`.md` opening with a tag is not a broken XML document, and saying so would be
124	noise. Hence `detection.Declared` — a parse failure is reported only when the
125	*name* claimed the kind.
126	
127	**A name declares in two ways, and the basename is read first.** `Dockerfile`
128	carries no extension at all, and `Dockerfile.dev` carries `.dev` — which is in no
129	table, so an extension-first lookup would settle it as plain text before the name
130	was ever read. Hence `basenameKinds` and the `dockerfile.` prefix ahead of
131	`extensionKinds`. A dotfile goes the other way round and lands in the extension
132	table, because Go's `filepath.Ext(".bashrc")` returns the whole name; which table
133	holds it is an implementation detail, that it is found is not.
134	
135	**The shebang is the one exception, and it is written down as one** — in
136	`sniff()`, in `TestAShebangDeclaresAShellScript`, and here. `#!/usr/bin/env bash`
137	is not an indication of what a file resembles: it is the file naming the
138	interpreter it is to be run by, which is an extension's standing minus the
139	extension. It applies only where `sniff` already did — a file with no extension
140	at all — and only to a short list of shells, because answering a
141	`#!/usr/bin/env python` with the bash lexer would colour a Python file wrong,
142	which is worse than leaving it plain since it looks deliberate.
143	
144	**YAML, TOML, Dockerfiles and shell scripts are coloured, and have no tree.**
145	`Structured()` excludes YAML and TOML by decision, not by oversight: both have a
146	structure, but neither has a parser *here* that preserves the file's order, and
147	order is content (below). `yaml.v3` could do it — `yaml.Node` keeps order and
148	comments, and it is already a dependency — while TOML would cost another one.
149	Until that is worth doing they are text with the colour on, and `f` is hidden for
150	them (Rule 130). A Dockerfile and a shell script are not excluded from anything:
151	they are programs, and a program is read in its own order.
152	
153	The class mapping is **read off the lexers**, not guessed, and each kind added
154	has said something the guess would have missed:
155	
156	| Kind | What the reading found |
157	|---|---|
158	| YAML | nothing to do — keys arrive as `NameTag`, scalars as `Literal`, `true`/`null` as `KeywordConstant` |
159	| TOML | every key, table headers included, arrives as `NameOther`, which fell through to `ClassText` — a TOML coloured everywhere except the thing worth colouring |
160	| Markdown | the whole `Generic` category was unmapped, so a Markdown arrived very nearly colourless |
161	| Dockerfile, shell | instructions and `if`/`fi` arrive as a **bare `Keyword`**, and a shell variable as `NameVariable`, which fell through to ordinary text |
162	
163	Neither the JSON nor the XML lexer emits `NameOther`, so the mapping is not
164	guarded on the kind; the classification tests are what keep that true. No
165	dependency and no binary growth for any of it: chroma embeds every lexer already,
166	which is what the +4.0 MB below bought.
167	
168	**`Keyword` and `KeywordConstant` are separated, and the test is equality.**
169	`KeywordConstant` is `true`, `false`, `null` — a value, so `ClassLiteral`; every
170	other keyword is a word of the language, so `ClassKeyword`. The split could not
171	disturb what already worked, and that is checked rather than hoped: the JSON,
172	YAML, TOML and XML lexers emit `KeywordConstant` and never a bare `Keyword`, and
173	`TestAKeywordConstantIsStillALiteral` is what keeps it so. Written the obvious
174	way it would have been wrong — chroma implements a sub-category as
175	`t/100 == other/100`, so `InSubCategory(KeywordConstant)` answers **true for every
176	keyword there is** and silently swallows the other branch. `ColorSyntaxKeyword`
177	aliases `ColorPrimary`, the literal's colour: invisible in the default theme, and
178	a name for a theme that wants to separate them — the argument already made for
179	`ColorFooterError` against `ColorError`.
180	
181	**Five classes carry a text attribute rather than a colour**, and Markdown is why:
182	once the rendered display has taken the `**` and the `~~` away, weight and
183	strikethrough are the only thing left saying two runs were ever different, and a
184	hue would say it less — a bold word is bold in any theme. `ClassStrong`,
185	`ClassEmph` and `ClassStrike` therefore keep `ColorText` and set `Bold`, `Italic`
186	and `Strikethrough`; `ClassHeading` takes `ColorSyntaxHeading` and bold both.
187	They still set a background like every other style (Rule 115), which is exactly
188	what an attribute-only style invites you to forget —
189	`TestEveryRenderedStyleCarriesTheAppBackground` asks each of them directly.
190	
191	**`Tokenize` coalesces adjacent runs of one class**, and that is not tidiness. The
192	markdown lexer ends its inline rules with a catch-all single-character
193	alternative, so ordinary prose comes back **one token per character**: at the
194	5 MiB `MaxSize` ceiling that is millions of `Token` values for a paragraph that
195	is a handful of runs. `TestAdjacentRunsOfOneClassAreCoalesced` counts them. It
196	preserves the concatenation invariant — only the boundaries move — and drops the
197	empty runs several lexers emit between groups. `Match` is deliberately not
198	consulted: `Tokenize` never sets it, `MarkMatches` does, after the filter.
199	
200	**Order is content.** Both parsers read a token stream (`json.Decoder.Token`,
201	`xml.Decoder.Token`), never a decoded value: `map[string]any` loses the file's
202	order. That is also why the tree's columns declare **neither `Less` nor
203	`Search`** — sorting would destroy what the parser took care to keep, and a text
204	filter would hide parents and orphan their children. `.` and `/` are unbound in
205	the tree, and Rule 138 says so by omission.
206	
207	**The tree is a `datatable`, the text pane a `viewport`.** The tree qualifies for
208	a reason worth stating: **a tree cell carries exactly one syntax class**, so one
209	`Style` per cell is enough — `datatable` cannot express several colours in one
210	cell and never has to here. The text pane is not a table, so Rule 122 does not
211	apply; Rule 115 does, and every token style sets its background.
212	
213	**Wrapping happens on tokens, never on coloured text.** A styled line cannot be
214	cut: the measure counts an escape's bytes as width and the cut lands inside the
215	sequence — Rule 122's hazard, one layer up. `docLine` keeps a line as spans,
216	`wrapTokens` splits it while it is still plain, and the colour goes on after.
217	
218	**chroma is a lexer and nothing else.** Its formatters emit their own ANSI and
219	resets, and a reset mid-line takes the app background to the margin (Rule 115).
220	The `TokenType → TokenClass` mapping was **read off the lexers**, not guessed:
221	JSON and XML both emit `NameTag`, for a key and for a tag respectively, hence the
222	`kind` parameter.
223	The invariant everything rests on — concatenating the tokens reproduces the input
224	exactly — has a test of its own. Cost: **+4.0 MB** on the binary (19.9 → 24.0),
225	because chroma embeds every lexer.
226	
227	Syntax colours are **semantic aliases assigned in `ApplyTheme`**, like
228	`ColorChartBg`: no theme file gains a key. Log levels get none —
229	`StatusErrorStyle`, `StatusWarningStyle` and `DimStyle` already mean that.
230	`ColorSearchMatch`/`Fg` are the same kind of alias.
231	
232	**A search filters and highlights, and one rule decides both.** `MatchRanges` is
233	the only thing that says a line matched, and it says *where* in the same answer:
234	the filter is `len(ranges) > 0`, so "a line the search kept carries at least one
235	highlighted occurrence" holds by construction. Two calculations for one question
236	is what `scan.Categorize` and `Result.SecretVerdict` each had to undo, and the
237	symptom was identical both times — something counted in one place and absent from
238	the other. Here it would be a line kept with nothing visible in it.
239	
240	The consequences, each with a test:
241	
242	- **A match is one more span, never a colour laid over a finished line.**
243	  `MarkMatches` cuts the tokens while they are still plain, for the reason
244	  `docLine` exists at all. It runs *after* the filter, so only on the lines about
245	  to be drawn, and it keeps Tokenize's byte-for-byte invariant.
246	- **`matchStyle` overrides the class and the level both.** A log line comes out as
247	  level, match, level: the level still carries the rest of it, so an ERROR is
248	  still picked out at a glance, and a search invisible in a log would be missing
249	  precisely where the lines are longest.
250	- **`c` has no say over it.** An occurrence is not syntax colouring; turning the
251	  colours off is how someone reads a document as plain text, and a search they
252	  then could not see would be the one thing that cost them.
253	- **Cutting a token copies it** (`withText`, `appendSpan`) rather than rebuilding
254	  a literal. A literal has to name every field to keep it, which is how a
255	  highlight works right up until the line is long enough to wrap — the one case it
256	  exists for. Byte offsets, not runes: a token holds a string. And when
257	  `strings.ToLower` changes a string's length in bytes (`İ`), the search falls
258	  back to a case-sensitive one rather than pointing beside the match.
259	- **The case is a parameter of that same call** (`s`, §3.53), never a second
260	  reading in the view. It decides which lines survive *and* which spans are
261	  highlighted, so a filter consulting the flag on its own would be exactly the
262	  second calculation the rule above exists to prevent. It re-filters the query
263	  already in force rather than clearing it: comparing the two readings is the
264	  whole reason to press the key. The `İ` guard belongs to the folding branch
265	  alone — the sensitive one never folds, so it has nothing to be exact about.
266	
267	**The bar carries what is filtering, and the two tokens are built together.**
268	`syncFilterTokens` emits the verbosity token and the `Aa` token in one pass
269	rather than each toggle setting its own: the bar disappears when nothing is
270	active (Rule 136), so what has to be right is *which tokens exist at all*, and
271	that is one question with one answer.
272	
273	**Line numbers are the document's, and the gutter is not text** (§3.53). `n`
274	draws them, `docLine.Num` carries them, posted once in `buildLines`. Four things
275	follow, each with a test:
276	
277	- **A filtered pane does not renumber.** The numbers keep gaps where a search or
278	  a verbosity dropped lines — that is the only reading that lets a line be quoted
279	  by its number, and it is what the gutter is for.
280	- **The gutter is not searchable, by construction.** It never enters
281	  `docLine.Plain`, so `MatchRanges` cannot see it. The cheap implementation —
282	  prefix, then filter — would pass every other test of the feature.
283	- **The gutter comes off the width before the wrap**, not after. `wrapTokens`
284	  counts runes and knows nothing about what is put in front of a segment, so
285	  wrapping at the full width and prefixing afterwards pushes every row past the
286	  right margin by exactly the gutter — on every line, which reads as a border
287	  fault rather than as a gutter one.
288	- **A wrapped line numbers its first row only.** A number says where a source
289	  line *begins*; repeating it would claim the document holds several lines
290	  bearing the same one. Dim, like every other value that is on every row.
291	
292	**`g` goes to a line, and refuses twice rather than doing something adjacent.**
293	The prompt is a **mode**: it claims every key before the pane sees one, the way a
294	confirmation modal does, so a digit cannot also scroll and `esc` closes it rather
295	than leaving the viewer. `rowOfLine`, rebuilt with the pane, is the only thing
296	that knows where a document line landed — a row is not a line once a filter has
297	dropped some and a wrap has split others — and it holds the **first** row of a
298	wrapped line, so a jump never lands inside one.
299	
300	| The number | What happens |
301	|---|---|
302	| empty | nothing, in silence — a change of mind, not a mistake |
303	| past the end | `Document has N lines` |
304	| hidden by the filter | `Line N is hidden by the filter`, and **nothing moves** |
305	| on screen | that line goes to the top of the pane, as `less` does |
306	
307	The hidden case is the one worth keeping written down: scrolling to the nearest
308	visible line would report success while putting a different number under the
309	cursor, which is D20's shape — an absence rendered as something else. The user
310	can lift the filter, or not.
311	
312	**The prompt takes the filter bar's slot, exclusively.** Both are one line inside
313	`components.BarFrame` — extracted from `FilterBar.View()`, so the rectangle that
314	closes the viewport has one implementation — and `GetFooterHeight` answers 2
315	either way. That is what stops the pane resizing under the reader when the prompt
316	opens over an active search. `InEditMode` and `FilterBarVisible` both count it.
317	
318	**`g` was a retired vim alias, and it came back with a different meaning.**
319	§3.26 removed `g`/`G` as aliases of `home`/`end`; here the letter opens a prompt
320	and the jump takes an **argument**, which is precisely what `home` and `end` do
321	not cover. So it leaves `keymap_test.go`'s `retiredAliases`, with its reason
322	written there — the shape of `H` returning to `free` in §3.47, taken the other
323	way round. `j` and `k` stay retired: they are `down` and `up` under another name.
324	
325	Three key collisions were resolved rather than accepted: follow moved `f` →
326	`F` (`ctrl+r` and `F` read as *reload once* / *keep reloading*); `h`/`l` are
327	unbound because no bare letter is navigation and no lowercase letter acts
328	(§3.26), hence `c` for coloration; and `q` closes nothing — it is the
329	application's quit key, and the logs pane was the one screen that ate it.
330	
331	**What this deleted.** The containers logs pane — `viewState`, its `viewport`,
332	wrap, ANSI stripping, scroll keys, reload, follow, timestamps and the external
333	pager — moved here whole; `containers/update.go` went from 707 to 548 lines.
334	`wrapLines` and the ANSI/CR normalisation were **moved**, comments included:
335	their reasons apply to any text this application shows. Every `docker inspect`
336	pager path is gone, Windows temp files included. `V` survives for logs alone,
337	because `less` handles a gigabyte and follows it.
338	
339	**`PagerCmd` carries no quote, on either branch.** Go's `exec.Command` escapes
340	an argument's inner quotes as `\"` when it builds a Windows command line, and
341	`cmd.exe` does not understand that escaping — it reads the backslashes as part
342	of the path. So `more "%TEMP%\devdesk-logs.txt"` reached cmd as
343	`C:\C:\Users\...\devdesk-logs.txt\`, which it refused, and `V` returned to
344	DevDesk instantly with an exit status nobody rendered: on Windows the pager
345	never once worked. Measured by running the exact string through
346	`exec.Command`, not deduced.
347	
348	The temp file went with the quotes, because its stated reason was false: **`more`
349	reads a pipe** — `dir | more` is its canonical use. The two branches now differ
350	only in the shell and the pager's name, nothing touches disk, and no path needs
351	quoting. The container ID is still interpolated into a shell string, which is
352	safe only because it comes from `docker ps`; do not extend that to a value the
353	user types.
354	
355	A failed pager is now **reported** (`Pager failed — check logs`). One that
356	cannot start comes back in milliseconds and is indistinguishable from one the
357	user quit at once, which is exactly how a command line broken since the day it
358	was written went unnoticed — the log line was there all along, and nobody reads
359	a log to find out why a key did nothing.

3	// CertState is what a monitored certificate is, as opposed to what a service
4	// is. A service is reachable or it is not; a certificate has a date, so it
5	// has one more state — the one where it is still valid and already demands
6	// action.
7	//
8	// That is why certificates cannot borrow the monitors' vocabulary.
9	// `up` / `down` / `error` lumped together three facts that are not handled
10	// the same way: an expired certificate (the service is already broken), a
11	// certificate due for renewal (it is not broken yet, and this is the only
12	// moment where action can be taken), and a certificate that could not be
13	// read (nothing is known). The third is the only one that is truly an
14	// error.
15	type CertState string
16	
17	const (
18		// CertValid — read, and far from its expiry.
19		CertValid CertState = "valid"
20		// CertToRenew — read, still valid, and inside the renewal window.
21		CertToRenew CertState = "to renew"
22		// CertExpired — read, and its date has passed.
23		CertExpired CertState = "expired"
24		// CertError — not read at all: unreachable host, refused handshake,
25		// empty chain, target not configured. This is an absence of a
26		// measurement, not a verdict on the certificate.
27		CertError CertState = "error"
28	)
29	
30	// CertRenewWindowDays is where a certificate stops being a date and becomes a
31	// task. It matches SSLChecker's `WARNING` window: the two answer the same
32	// question, and two diverging thresholds would make the dashboard say
33	// `to renew` about something `:status` still shows in green.
34	const CertRenewWindowDays = 30
35	
36	// CertStateOf classifies one monitored certificate.
37	//
38	// It is decided from `SSLDaysLeft` and not from `Status`, because
39	// `StatusType` does not have four values to give: SSLChecker returns
40	// `ERROR` both for an expired certificate and for one expiring in six days,
41	// and `DOWN` for an unreachable host. The number of days, on the other
42	// hand, distinguishes the three — and its absence is exactly the case where
43	// nothing could be read.
44	func CertStateOf(c ComponentStatus) CertState {
45		if c.SSLDaysLeft == nil {
46			return CertError
47		}
48		switch days := *c.SSLDaysLeft; {
49		case days < 0:
50			return CertExpired
51		case days <= CertRenewWindowDays:
52			return CertToRenew
53		default:
54			return CertValid
55		}
56	}
57	
58	// CertCounts tallies a set of monitored certificates, one figure per state.
59	func CertCounts(certs []ComponentStatus) (valid, toRenew, expired, errored int) {
60		for _, c := range certs {
61			switch CertStateOf(c) {
62			case CertValid:
63				valid++
64			case CertToRenew:
65				toRenew++
66			case CertExpired:
67				expired++
68			case CertError:
69				errored++
70			}
71		}
72		return
73	}

8	// detection is what the name and the content managed to say about a document.
9	//
10	// Declared separates "the name said JSON" from "the content started with a
11	// brace". Only the first is worth reporting a parse failure for: a Markdown
12	// file that happens to open with a tag is not a broken XML document, and
13	// telling the user it is would be noise about a file that is displaying fine.
14	type detection struct {
15		Kind     Kind
16		Declared bool
17	}

19	// extensionKinds are the extensions that decide, on their own, what a file is.
20	//
21	// A log, a YAML, a TOML, a Markdown, a Dockerfile and a shell script are only
22	// ever recognised here, by basename below, or declared by their producer — never
23	// sniffed from the content. "This looks like a log" is not a decidable question,
24	// and neither is "this looks like YAML": the registry `provider` field is the
25	// precedent, declared and never inferred from the URL, so nothing depends on
26	// what happened to be seen first.
27	var extensionKinds = map[string]Kind{
28		".json":     KindJSON,
29		".xml":      KindXML,
30		".log":      KindLog,
31		".yaml":     KindYAML,
32		".yml":      KindYAML,
33		".toml":     KindTOML,
34		".md":       KindMarkdown,
35		".markdown": KindMarkdown,
36		".mkd":      KindMarkdown,
37		".sh":       KindShell,
38		".bash":     KindShell,
39		".zsh":      KindShell,
40		".ksh":      KindShell,
41	
42		// A file named `web.dockerfile` — the form a repository holding several of
43		// them uses, since only one file per directory can be called Dockerfile.
44		".dockerfile": KindDockerfile,
45	
46		// Go's filepath.Ext returns the whole name for a dotfile: Ext(".bashrc") is
47		// ".bashrc". Listing them here rather than as basenames is not a shortcut,
48		// it is where the lookup will actually find them.
49		".bashrc":       KindShell,
50		".zshrc":        KindShell,
51		".profile":      KindShell,
52		".bash_profile": KindShell,
53		".zprofile":     KindShell,
54	}
55	
56	// basenameKinds are the files whose *whole name* is the declaration, because
57	// they carry no extension to declare anything with.
58	//
59	// It has to be consulted before the extension, not after: `Dockerfile.dev` has
60	// the extension ".dev", which is in no table, so an extension-first lookup would
61	// settle it as plain text before the basename ever got a say.
62	var basenameKinds = map[string]Kind{
63		"dockerfile":    KindDockerfile,
64		"containerfile": KindDockerfile,
65	}
66	
67	// dockerfilePrefix catches the `Dockerfile.dev` / `Dockerfile.prod` family. It
68	// is a prefix rule rather than more entries because the suffix is arbitrary —
69	// it is whatever the project calls that build.
70	const dockerfilePrefix = "dockerfile."

72	// DetectKind is what a document is, judged by its name and then its content.
73	func DetectKind(name string, data []byte) Kind {
74		return detect(name, data).Kind
75	}
76	
77	func detect(name string, data []byte) detection {
78		base := strings.ToLower(filepath.Base(name))
79		if kind, ok := basenameKinds[base]; ok {
80			return detection{Kind: kind, Declared: true}
81		}
82		if strings.HasPrefix(base, dockerfilePrefix) {
83			return detection{Kind: KindDockerfile, Declared: true}
84		}
85	
86		ext := strings.ToLower(filepath.Ext(name))
87		if kind, ok := extensionKinds[ext]; ok {
88			return detection{Kind: kind, Declared: true}
89		}
90		// Any other extension is taken at its word: a .go or a .txt is text, and
91		// sniffing it would open a Go file as a tree the first time someone started
92		// one with a brace.
93		if ext != "" {
94			return detection{Kind: KindPlain}
95		}
96		return detection{Kind: sniff(data)}
97	}
98	
99	// leadingNoise is what may sit in front of a document's first real character:
100	// whitespace, and a byte-order mark an editor left behind. Without the mark in
101	// this set, a BOM would hide the very byte this function exists to read.
102	const leadingNoise = " \t\r\n\ufeff"
103	
104	// sniff guesses at a file with no extension at all — a Makefile, a hook, a dump
105	// someone redirected into a name. It looks at the first meaningful byte and
106	// nothing else; a document that then fails to parse simply falls back to text,
107	// with no complaint, because nothing claimed it was structured.
108	//
109	// Only JSON and XML are guessed at, and only because a leading brace or tag is
110	// the whole of the question. YAML and TOML are never sniffed: a file opening
111	// with `---` is not thereby YAML, and `[section]` is a line of prose in half the
112	// files that contain one.
113	//
114	// A shebang is the exception, and it is one worth writing down rather than
115	// leaving to be rediscovered as drift. `#!/usr/bin/env bash` is not an
116	// indication of what the file resembles: it is the file naming the interpreter
117	// it is to be run by, which is the most explicit declaration a script can carry
118	// — the same standing as an extension, minus the extension. Contrast `---`,
119	// which is Markdown front matter as often as it is a YAML stream.
120	func sniff(data []byte) Kind {
121		head := data
122		if len(head) > sniffSize {
123			head = head[:sniffSize]
124		}
125		trimmed := strings.TrimLeft(string(head), leadingNoise)
126		switch {
127		case strings.HasPrefix(trimmed, "{"), strings.HasPrefix(trimmed, "["):
128			return KindJSON
129		case strings.HasPrefix(trimmed, "<"):
130			return KindXML
131		case shellShebang(trimmed):
132			return KindShell
133		default:
134			return KindPlain
135		}
136	}
137	
138	// shellInterpreters are the shebang interpreters this viewer colours as shell.
139	//
140	// The list is short on purpose: a `#!/usr/bin/env python` is a shebang too, and
141	// answering it with the bash lexer would colour a Python file wrong — which is
142	// worse than leaving it plain, because it looks deliberate.
143	var shellInterpreters = []string{"sh", "bash", "zsh", "ksh", "dash", "ash"}
144	
145	// shellShebang reports whether a document opens with a shell interpreter line.
146	func shellShebang(trimmed string) bool {
147		if !strings.HasPrefix(trimmed, "#!") {
148			return false
149		}
150		line := trimmed
151		if end := strings.IndexAny(line, "\r\n"); end >= 0 {
152			line = line[:end]
153		}
154		// The interpreter is the last path segment of the line: "#!/bin/bash" and
155		// "#!/usr/bin/env bash -e" both end up at "bash" once the arguments and the
156		// directories are taken off.
157		for _, field := range strings.Fields(line) {
158			name := field
159			if idx := strings.LastIndexAny(name, "/\\"); idx >= 0 {
160				name = name[idx+1:]
161			}
162			for _, interpreter := range shellInterpreters {
163				if name == interpreter {
164					return true
165				}
166			}
167		}
168		return false
169	}

27	func (s *SSLChecker) Check(ctx context.Context, component config.ComponentConfig) ComponentStatus {
28		result := ComponentStatus{
29			Name:      component.Name,
30			Type:      TypeSSL,
31			Target:    component.Target,
32			Timestamp: time.Now(),
33		}
34	
35		if component.Target == "" {
36			result.Status = StatusError
37			result.Error = "target not configured"
38			return result
39		}
40	
41		// Parse target - add :443 if no port specified
42		host := component.Target
43		if !strings.Contains(host, ":") {
44			host = host + ":443"
45		}
46	
47		// Create TLS dialer with timeout
48		dialer := &net.Dialer{
49			Timeout: s.timeout,
50		}
51	
52		// Measure connection time
53		start := time.Now()
54		conn, err := tls.DialWithDialer(dialer, "tcp", host, &tls.Config{
55			InsecureSkipVerify: false, // Validate certificates
56		})
57		result.ResponseTime = time.Since(start)
58	
59		if err != nil {
60			result.Status = StatusDown
61			result.Error = err.Error()
62			return result
63		}
64		defer func() { _ = conn.Close() }()
65	
66		// Get certificate chain
67		certs := conn.ConnectionState().PeerCertificates
68		if len(certs) == 0 {
69			result.Status = StatusError
70			result.Error = "no certificates found"
71			return result
72		}
73	
74		// Use leaf certificate (first in chain)
75		cert := certs[0]
76	
77		// Extract certificate data
78		notAfter := cert.NotAfter
79		issuer := cert.Issuer.CommonName
80		if issuer == "" {
81			// Fallback to Organization if CommonName is empty
82			if len(cert.Issuer.Organization) > 0 {
83				issuer = cert.Issuer.Organization[0]
84			} else {
85				issuer = "Unknown"
86			}
87		}
88		daysLeft := int(time.Until(notAfter).Hours() / 24)
89	
90		// Populate SSL-specific fields
91		result.SSLExpires = &notAfter
92		result.SSLDaysLeft = &daysLeft
93		result.SSLIssuer = issuer
94	
95		// Determine status based on days left
96		if daysLeft < 0 {
97			result.Status = StatusError
98			result.Error = "certificate expired"
99		} else if daysLeft < 7 {
100			result.Status = StatusError
101			result.Error = fmt.Sprintf("expires in %d days", daysLeft)
102		} else if daysLeft <= CertRenewWindowDays {
103			result.Status = StatusWarning
104			result.Error = fmt.Sprintf("expires in %d days", daysLeft)
105		} else {
106			result.Status = StatusOK
107		}
108	
109		return result

- **`internal/status/certificate_text.go`** — `FormatCertificateChain` renders each certificate's subject, issuer, serial, validity window, signature/key info, SANs, SHA-256 fingerprint, and its PEM block.
- **`internal/ui/status/sources.go`** — new `certSource` (`viewer.Source`, `Kind() = viewer.KindPlain`) that re-dials the monitor's target and formats the chain, following the same pattern as `containers`' `inspectSource`/`logsSource`.
- **`internal/ui/status/update.go`** — `enter` on the SSL Certificates tab opens the selected certificate's chain via `uiviewer.OpenRequestMsg` (mirrors how `enter` already opens a file/inspect elsewhere); no-op on the Monitors tab or with nothing selected.
- **`internal/ui/status/view.go`** — advertises `enter → Open certificate` only while the Certificates tab is active (Rule 138), and documents it in the help content.

Since the document is plain text, `Y` (copy) and everything else the viewer already provides work for free — no new viewer machinery was needed. Added tests for the formatter (self-signed chain via `x509.CreateCertificate`) and for the new source; full build, vet, and test suite pass.
